body:
Folk and tribal painting as living heritage

Gujarat possesses several traditions of painting that are closely connected with community life, religious beliefs, agriculture, festivals and domestic ceremonies. Unlike paintings produced primarily for galleries or royal courts, many traditional paintings are created as part of worship, thanksgiving or auspicious occasions.

Folk painting refers broadly to painting traditions transmitted within local communities through customary practice. Tribal painting refers to painting traditions associated with particular tribal or Adivasi communities and their cultural beliefs. These categories often overlap.

A ritual painting may represent a deity, fulfil a religious vow, seek protection or mark an important occasion. Its significance lies not only in its appearance but also in the beliefs, customs and knowledge associated with its creation.

Community and geographical distribution

Pithora painting, also known as Pithoro painting, is a traditional ritual wall painting particularly associated with the Rathwa or Rathva tribal community of eastern Gujarat.

Chhota Udepur and Panchmahal districts are important centres of this tradition. Related Pithora traditions also occur among tribal communities in neighbouring Madhya Pradesh, particularly in the Jhabua region.

Within Gujarat, the art is especially associated with the agricultural and religious life of the Rathwa community. The tradition preserves community beliefs, accounts of ancestors, religious narratives and representations of the natural environment.

Worship of Baba Pithora

Baba Pithora occupies a central position among the deities worshipped by the Rathwas. He is associated with food grains, agricultural prosperity and the well-being of the household.

A family experiencing illness, agricultural difficulties, problems related to livestock or other hardships may undertake a religious vow seeking the blessings of Baba Pithora. When the desired benefit is obtained, the family may commission a Pithora painting as an act of thanksgiving and fulfilment of the vow.

Votive painting

A votive painting is a painting created as a religious offering, often in fulfilment of a vow or in gratitude for a blessing believed to have been received. Pithora is an important example of votive tribal painting.

Participants in the tradition

The creation of a traditional Pithora involves distinct responsibilities within the community.

ParticipantTraditional responsibility
GhardhaniHouseholder who commissions the painting and undertakes the vow
Badva or BadwaReligious specialist who guides and supervises the ritual
LakharaTraditional painter responsible for creating the Pithora

The Badva possesses knowledge of community rituals and religious narratives. The Lakhara possesses the artistic knowledge required to represent these narratives through traditional motifs. The responsibilities of the ritual specialist and the painter are therefore distinct.

Location within the traditional house

Pithora is traditionally painted on the interior walls of a Rathwa house, particularly in the entrance or verandah area known as the osari. An elaborate ritual arrangement commonly extends across 3 adjoining walls.

The painted space acquires religious significance for the household. Although Pithora-style paintings are also produced on paper and canvas for sale, these portable works do not necessarily serve the same ritual function as a painting installed in a house.

Prelims focus

  • Pithora painting is particularly associated with the Rathwa tribal community.
  • Chhota Udepur and Panchmahal are major centres in Gujarat.
  • Baba Pithora is associated with agricultural prosperity and household welfare.
  • A traditional Pithora may fulfil a religious vow.
  • Lakhara is the painter; Badva is the religious specialist.
  • Trap: Pithora is traditionally a wall painting, not primarily a painted textile.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, An Introduction to Indian Art – Part II, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 8, p. 134; Government of Gujarat, Chhota Udepur District, Culture and Heritage; Gujarat Tourism, Pithora Painting; Hanoz H. R. Patel, Sahapedia, Pithora of the Rathvas, sections on ritual participants and vows. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

title: Pithora Painting: Rathwa Community and Ritual Significance

body:
The importance of horse motifs

The most recognisable feature of Pithora painting is the repeated representation of brightly coloured horses and mounted figures. These horses are not merely decorative animals. Within Rathwa religious tradition, they may represent deities, ancestors and other beings belonging to the community's sacred world.

The religious narrative of Baba Pithora and his marriage to Pithori occupies an important place in the composition. The surrounding figures connect this narrative with the everyday experiences of the community.

Representation of the universe

A traditional Pithora composition expresses the Rathwa understanding of the universe. This symbolic representation of the structure of the universe is known as cosmography.

In a characteristic composition, an ornate wavy line separates the upper celestial region from the lower region associated with the earthly world.

Upper region

The upper part represents the divine or celestial world. It includes mounted deities, heavenly bodies such as the sun and moon, and beings associated with religious mythology.

Lower region

The lower part includes the wedding procession of Pithora, minor deities, royal figures, farmers, domestic animals and other representations of earthly existence.

The precise selection and arrangement of motifs may vary between paintings. However, the connection between the religious world and human life remains a characteristic feature.

Important motifs and their significance

  • Horses and horse riders: Represent deities, ancestors and participants in religious narratives.
  • Sun and moon: Represent celestial bodies and the wider universe.
  • Wedding procession: Represents the religious narrative of Pithora and Pithori.
  • Farmers and cattle: Reflect agriculture, livestock and rural livelihoods.
  • Tigers, elephants, camels, birds and trees: Represent elements of the natural environment, mythology and community life.

These motifs should be understood together. Agricultural activities appear alongside religious figures because the community's beliefs are closely connected with the land, seasonal cycles, household welfare and prosperity.

Traditional surface and colours

Pithora is traditionally executed on a prepared wall. White clay used in preparing the painting surface is known as Pandu. In documented Rathwa rituals, unmarried girls of the household participate in applying this preparation.

The painting itself is traditionally executed by male Lakharas. Traditional pigments are mixed with milk and liquor obtained from the flowers of the mahuda or mahua tree. Bamboo implements and brushes are used to apply the colours.

The use of multiple bright colours against a light background gives Pithora its distinctive appearance. This contrasts with the predominantly white geometric figures found in traditional Warli painting.

Traditional and contemporary forms

Traditional Pithora is integrated into household worship. Contemporary artists also produce Pithora-style works on paper and canvas for exhibitions, collectors and commercial markets.

This change in medium has helped make the art accessible outside its original domestic setting. However, the artistic style and the complete religious ceremony should not be treated as identical.

Recognising Pithora

Rows of colourful horses, mounted deities, a religious wedding procession and representations of rural life are stronger identifying features of Pithora than any fixed number of animals or colours.

Prelims focus

  • Horses and mounted figures are characteristic Pithora motifs.
  • The composition reflects Rathwa cosmography.
  • A wavy line commonly separates celestial and earthly regions.
  • Pandu is the white clay preparation applied to the wall.
  • Milk and mahuda liquor are associated with traditional pigment preparation.
  • Trap: The horse motifs have religious significance and are not merely representations of animals.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, An Introduction to Indian Art – Part II, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 8, Pithoro Painting, p. 134; Gujarat Tourism, Pithora Painting; Government of Gujarat, Chhota Udepur District, Culture and Heritage; Sahapedia, Pithora of the Rathvas and Motifs in Pithora Painting. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning and purpose

Mata-ni-Pachhedi, also written as Mata ni Pachedi or Mata ni Pachhadi, is a traditional religious textile art of Gujarat. The name refers to a cloth placed behind the Mother Goddess.

The cloth carries painted and printed representations of a goddess, her worshippers, religious narratives and decorative motifs. It serves as a sacred backdrop in a shrine devoted to the Mother Goddess.

Mata-ni-Pachhedi

A sacred textile traditionally decorated through hand painting and block printing, used particularly as a backdrop for the worship of the Mother Goddess.

Traditional creators and centres

The traditional creators of Mata-ni-Pachhedi belong to the Devi Pujak or Devipujak community, historically also referred to as the Vaghari or Vaghri community.

The term Devi Pujak means a worshipper of the goddess. Artisan families practising the painting tradition are also known as Chitaras, a term associated with painters.

Ahmedabad, particularly artisan settlements associated with the Sabarmati River and the Vasana area, is an important centre of the tradition.

The art developed in close association with community worship rather than as a tradition of royal portraiture. The artisans transmitted their knowledge of religious images, textile decoration and traditional dyes within their families.

Portable shrines and ritual use

Historically, members of the community used decorated textiles to establish temporary places of worship. A painted cloth could be carried to another location, unlike a religious image painted directly on a permanent wall.

The textiles provided a sacred setting for the worship of the Mother Goddess even when a permanent shrine was unavailable.

Mata-ni-Pachhedi and related sacred textiles are used during Navratri, Dashama worship and other ceremonies associated with local goddesses. Devotees may also offer a decorated cloth to a shrine in fulfilment of a religious vow.

Difference between Pachhedi and Chandarvo

Two related textile forms are associated with this tradition.

  • Mata-ni-Pachhedi: A sacred cloth traditionally hung behind the image or shrine of the Mother Goddess.
  • Mata-no-Chandarvo: A decorated textile traditionally suspended above the shrine as a canopy.

Both forms may use similar religious imagery and methods of textile decoration. Their basic distinction concerns their position and function within the shrine. In practice, related cloths may also be adapted to different ritual arrangements.

Why it is called the Kalamkari of Gujarat

Mata-ni-Pachhedi is sometimes described as the Kalamkari of Gujarat because it involves drawing and painting on cloth with a pen-like implement known as a kalam. The tradition also uses carved wooden blocks to print certain designs.

Kalamkari literally refers to pen work. The term is also used for established textile painting and printing traditions associated with Andhra Pradesh. The religious subjects, artisan communities and regional identities of these traditions are distinct.

Prelims focus

  • The traditional creators of Mata-ni-Pachhedi are the Devi Pujaks.
  • Ahmedabad and the Sabarmati region are important centres.
  • The principal religious subject is the Mother Goddess.
  • Pachhedi traditionally serves as a shrine backdrop; Chandarvo serves as a canopy.
  • Mata-ni-Pachhedi is associated with Navratri and other goddess-worship rituals.
  • Trap: Mata-ni-Pachhedi is a textile painting and printing tradition, not a form of permanent wall mural.

[References: Gujarat Tourism, Mata Ni Pachhedi, updated 2 November 2026; Sandeep Joshi, Sahapedia, Kalamkari of Gujarat: Mata ni Pachhedi, sections on the Vaghri community and religious concerns; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Mapping of Indian Textiles, Mata-ni-Pachhedi. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

title: Mata-ni-Pachhedi: Sacred Textile Painting of the Devi Pujak Community

body:
Characteristic visual arrangement

A traditional Mata-ni-Pachhedi generally consists of a rectangular cotton cloth with a prominent representation of the Mother Goddess at its centre. Smaller figures, narrative scenes and decorative patterns occupy the surrounding areas.

The central goddess is frequently depicted on her vahana, meaning her associated vehicle or mount. The vahana helps worshippers identify the particular goddess represented in the painting.

The cloth may be divided into several compartments containing devotees, ancestors, religious scenes, animals and vegetation. Decorative borders frame the composition. The number and arrangement of compartments can vary according to the artist and the intended ritual use.

Traditional colours and materials

The most characteristic traditional colour scheme consists of red or maroon, black and the uncoloured white ground of the cloth.

Red and black are the principal applied colours in the traditional style. The white areas are generally retained by leaving portions of the fabric uncoloured.

Material or colourTraditional association
CottonPrincipal painting surface
BlackPrepared traditionally using iron-based ingredients
Red or maroonTraditionally associated with madder-type colouring substances and alum
WhiteUncoloured portions of the cloth
HardeMyrobalan used in preparing the cloth to receive colour

Artisans use freehand painting with a kalam and printing with carved wooden blocks. Both methods may appear in a single textile. Some examples also use indigo, while contemporary artists employ a wider range of colours and commercially available textile paints.

Mother goddesses and their vehicles

Gujarat has numerous traditions of worship centred on local mother goddesses. In Mata-ni-Pachhedi, the identity of the goddess can frequently be recognised through the animal, bird or other vehicle accompanying her.

GoddessCharacteristic vahana
Khodiyar MataCrocodile
Bahuchara MataCock or rooster
Meladi MataGoat
DashamaCamel
Visat MataBuffalo
Vahanvati MataShip

These associations belong to familiar local religious representations. Variations may occur in particular narratives or regional traditions.

Surrounding motifs and their meaning

  • Worshippers: Express devotion to the central goddess.
  • Ancestors: Reflect the connection between family identity, community memory and worship.
  • Animals and birds: May represent vehicles of goddesses, participants in religious stories or elements of nature.
  • Floral and geometric borders: Organise and decorate the sacred composition.

The larger central image indicates the religious importance of the goddess. Smaller surrounding figures establish her relationship with the community and its devotional traditions.

Distinguishing Mata-ni-Pachhedi from Pithora

Both art forms may be associated with religious vows and thanksgiving. Their surfaces, communities and central religious subjects, however, differ.

Pithora is traditionally a Rathwa wall painting centred on Baba Pithora and a wider sacred universe represented through numerous colourful horses. Mata-ni-Pachhedi is a Devi Pujak textile tradition organised around the Mother Goddess and her religious narratives.

Prelims focus

  • Cotton is the traditional surface of Mata-ni-Pachhedi.
  • Black and red are its characteristic traditional applied colours.
  • Hand painting and wooden block printing are both used.
  • The Mother Goddess and her vahana commonly occupy the central position.
  • Khodiyar is associated with the crocodile; Bahuchara with the cock; Dashama with the camel.
  • Trap: Traditional colour preferences do not mean that every contemporary Pachhedi is restricted to black and red.

[References: Gujarat Tourism, Mata Ni Pachhedi and Hidden Treasures of Gujarat, pp. 18–19; Sandeep Joshi, Sahapedia, Kalamkari of Gujarat: Mata ni Pachhedi, sections on local mother goddesses and materials; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Mapping of Indian Textiles, Mata-ni-Pachhedi. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]
